title: Chemical Thermodynamics

toc.title: 11.1 Systems and surroundings; state functions; internal energy; intensive and extensive properties; the first law and enthalpy
11.2 Enthalpies of reaction, formation, combustion, neutralisation, solution, fusion and vaporisation; Laplace's and Hess's laws
11.3 Spontaneity, entropy and the second law; Gibbs free energy and its relation to the equilibrium constant

html:
Thermodynamics answers a different question from kinetics: not how fast, but will it happen at all, and how much heat is involved. The paper carries about one question from this chapter (our estimate from the MEC topic list).

It is usually a Hess's-law addition, a \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S sign decision, or a definition question about the enthalpy of formation, combustion or neutralisation.

The marks are lost on three things: a sign convention applied inconsistently, a non-zero enthalpy of formation for an element, and the belief that "spontaneous" means "fast".

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • System and surroundings; open, closed and isolated systems; state functions (U, H, S, G) against path functions (q, w); intensive against extensive.
  • First law in the IUPAC convention: \Delta U = q + w, with q positive when heat enters the system and w positive when work is done on it; w = -P\Delta V.
  • H = U + PV; \Delta H = q_p and \Delta U = q_v; \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT.
  • \Delta H_f^\circ of an element in its standard state is zero; \Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{reactants}).
  • Laplace's law: \Delta H reverses sign when a reaction is reversed. Hess's law: \Delta H is independent of the path, so equations may be added and subtracted.
  • Second law: \Delta S_{\text{universe}} > 0 for a spontaneous change. Entropy rises from solid to liquid to gas.
  • \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S; \Delta G < 0 spontaneous, = 0 equilibrium, > 0 non-spontaneous. The four sign cases decide the temperature behaviour.
  • \Delta G^\circ = -RT \ln K; negative \Delta G^\circ means K > 1.

11.1 Systems and surroundings; state functions; internal energy; intensive and extensive properties; the first law and enthalpy

System, surroundings and the three types of system

System and surroundings

The system is the part of the universe under study; the surroundings are everything else; the boundary separates them and may be real (a beaker wall) or imaginary.

Type Exchanges matter? Exchanges energy? Example
Open yes yes water boiling in an open pan; a living cell
Closed no yes a sealed flask being heated; a piston-cylinder with no leak
Isolated no no a thermos flask; a bomb calorimeter (approximately)

An isolated system is the only one for which \Delta U = 0 always, because neither heat nor work can cross the boundary.

State functions and path functions

State function

A state function is a property whose value depends only on the present state of the system — its pressure, volume, temperature and composition — and not on how that state was reached.

Its change between two states is \Delta X = X_{\text{final}} - X_{\text{initial}} and is the same for every route.

State functions Path functions
internal energy U, enthalpy H, entropy S, free energy G heat q, work w
pressure P, volume V, temperature T, amount n —
A change depends only on the end points A value depends on the route taken

Because U is a state function, \Delta U for a change from A to B is fixed. But q and w are not: one route may exchange a lot of heat and little work, another the reverse. Only their sum is fixed, which is exactly what the first law says.

Intensive and extensive properties

Intensive and extensive

An extensive property depends on the amount of substance present — mass, volume, internal energy, enthalpy, entropy, free energy. An intensive property does not — temperature, pressure, density, molar volume, concentration, molar enthalpy, E^\circ.

Doubling the amount doubles every extensive property but leaves every intensive one unchanged. This is the same idea that makes E^\circ of an electrode independent of how the half-reaction is written (Unit 10), and it is why \Delta H is quoted per mole.

Extensive Intensive
mass, volume, n density, molar volume
U, H, S, G, C (heat capacity) T, P, molar heat capacity
\Delta H of a stated amount \Delta H_f^\circ per mole

Internal energy and the first law

The internal energy U is the total energy of the system — kinetic energy of its molecules plus the potential energy of their interactions. Its absolute value cannot be measured; only \Delta U can.

The first law of thermodynamics

Energy can be converted from one form to another but can neither be created nor destroyed. For a closed system:

\Delta U = q + w

where q is the heat supplied to the system and w the work done on the system. Both are positive when energy enters the system. This is the IUPAC convention and it is the one used throughout this book.

For expansion against a constant external pressure, the work done on the system is

w = -P_{\text{ext}}\Delta V

so an expanding gas (\Delta V > 0) has w < 0: it loses energy by doing work. A compressed gas has w > 0.

Change \Delta V w Meaning
Gas expands positive negative system does work on the surroundings
Gas compressed negative positive surroundings do work on the system
\Delta V = 0 zero 0 no pressure–volume work
Two conventions — read the stem

Some older textbooks write \Delta U = q - w and count work done by the system as positive. The physics is identical; only the book-keeping differs. If a question names the convention, follow it.

If it does not, use IUPAC (\Delta U = q + w) and remember that an expanding gas has negative work. Never mix the two within one calculation — that is where the "sign error" distractors come from.

First law with both signs

Problem. A gas absorbs 500 J of heat and does 200 J of work on the surroundings. Find \Delta U. Then find \Delta U if the same gas absorbs 500 J and has 200 J of work done on it.

Solution. IUPAC: q = +500 J. Work done by the system is negative: w = -200 J. \Delta U = 500 + (-200) = \mathbf{+300} J — the gas warms. Second case: w = +200 J, so \Delta U = 500 + 200 = \mathbf{+700} J.

Work of expansion in joules

Problem. A gas expands from 2.0 L to 4.0 L against a constant pressure of 1.0 atm. Find the work done on the system in joules (1 L atm = 101.3 J).

Solution. \Delta V = +2.0 L. w = -P\Delta V = -(1.0)(2.0) = -2.0 L atm = -2.0 \times 101.3 = \mathbf{-203} J. The negative sign says the system lost energy as work; the surroundings gained it.

Enthalpy

Most reactions in a laboratory are carried out in open vessels, at constant pressure, not constant volume. The heat exchanged then is not \Delta U, because the system also does work pushing back the atmosphere. Thermodynamics therefore defines a new state function:

H = U + PV

Enthalpy

Enthalpy H is the heat content of a system at constant pressure, defined as H = U + PV. At constant pressure the heat exchanged equals the change in enthalpy, q_p = \Delta H; at constant volume, q_v = \Delta U.

For a change at constant pressure, \Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V. For reactions involving gases, P\Delta V = \Delta n_g RT, where \Delta n_g is the change in the number of moles of gas:

\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT

  • If \Delta n_g = 0, \Delta H = \Delta U (e.g. H₂ + I₂ → 2HI).
  • If \Delta n_g < 0 (gas consumed), \Delta H < \Delta U — the reaction is more exothermic at constant pressure.
  • If \Delta n_g > 0 (gas produced), \Delta H > \Delta U.
Sign \Delta H Heat Example
Exothermic negative released to the surroundings combustion, neutralisation, condensation
Endothermic positive absorbed from the surroundings melting, boiling, decomposition of CaCO₃
Converting ΔU to ΔH

Problem. For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), \Delta U = -87.4 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Find \Delta H (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

Solution. \Delta n_g = 2 - (1 + 3) = -2. \Delta n_g RT = (-2)(8.314)(298) = -4955 J = -4.96 kJ. \Delta H = -87.4 + (-4.96) = \mathbf{-92.4} kJ mol⁻¹.

The reaction releases slightly more heat at constant pressure, because the surroundings do work on the system as four moles of gas collapse into two.

11.2 Enthalpies of reaction, formation, combustion, neutralisation, solution, fusion and vaporisation; Laplace's and Hess's laws

Enthalpy of reaction

The enthalpy of reaction \Delta H_r is the heat change when the reaction takes place as written, with the coefficients interpreted as moles. It is found from formation enthalpies:

\Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} = \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{products}) - \sum \Delta H_f^\circ(\text{reactants})

The logic: every compound is imagined broken into its elements (cost = -\Delta H_f^\circ), and the elements are reassembled into the products (gain = +\Delta H_f^\circ).

Enthalpy of formation

Standard enthalpy of formation

The standard enthalpy of formation \Delta H_f^\circ is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its elements in their standard states at 298 K and 1 bar. By definition it is zero for an element in its standard state.

Substance \Delta H_f^\circ (kJ mol⁻¹) Note
C(graphite), O₂(g), H₂(g), N₂(g), Br₂(l), I₂(s), Na(s) 0 standard states
C(diamond) +1.9 not the standard state of carbon
O₃(g) +142 not the standard state of oxygen
CH₄(g) −74.8
CO(g) −110.5
CO₂(g) −393.5
H₂O(l) −285.8
H₂O(g) −241.8 the difference is the enthalpy of vaporisation
NH₃(g) −46.1
C₂H₅OH(l) −277.7
Zero, but only for the standard state

\Delta H_f^\circ is zero for graphite, not diamond; for O₂ gas, not ozone; for rhombic sulphur, not monoclinic; for white phosphorus is not zero (red phosphorus is the standard state).

An option that says "the enthalpy of formation of every element is zero" is wrong — it is zero only in the most stable form at 298 K and 1 bar.

The other enthalpies, one by one

Enthalpy Definition (all per mole) Sign and typical value
Combustion \Delta H_c^\circ one mole of substance burnt completely in excess O₂ always negative for fuels; CH₄ −890.3 kJ mol⁻¹
Neutralisation \Delta H_n^\circ one mole of H⁺ from an acid neutralised by OH⁻ from a base −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹ for strong acid + strong base
Solution \Delta H_{\text{sol}}^\circ one mole of substance dissolved in enough solvent that further dilution gives no heat change NaOH −44.5; NH₄NO₃ +25.7 (endothermic, the cold pack)
Fusion \Delta H_{\text{fus}}^\circ one mole of solid melted at its melting point always positive; ice +6.01 kJ mol⁻¹
Vaporisation \Delta H_{\text{vap}}^\circ one mole of liquid boiled at its boiling point always positive; water +40.7 kJ mol⁻¹
Sublimation \Delta H_{\text{sub}}^\circ one mole of solid converted directly to vapour positive; equals \Delta H_{\text{fus}} + \Delta H_{\text{vap}}

Why neutralisation is always about −57 kJ. A strong acid and a strong base are fully ionised, so whatever the acid and base, the reaction is the same:

H^+(aq) + OH^-(aq) \rightarrow H_2O(l) \qquad \Delta H = -57.1\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}

A weak acid or base gives a smaller (less negative) value, because some of the energy released is used up in ionising the weak electrolyte. This is a favourite distractor: the value is −57.1 for strong–strong only.

Enthalpy of solution is the sum of two terms: the lattice enthalpy (energy needed to break the crystal apart, endothermic) and the hydration enthalpy (energy released when the ions are surrounded by water, exothermic).

When hydration wins, dissolution is exothermic (NaOH); when the lattice wins, it is endothermic (NH₄NO₃, KNO₃).

Laplace's law

Laplace's law

The enthalpy change of a reaction is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to that of the reverse reaction: \Delta H_{\text{forward}} = -\Delta H_{\text{backward}}.

So if the formation of water releases 285.8 kJ per mole, the decomposition of one mole of liquid water into its elements absorbs exactly 285.8 kJ. Nothing is lost in the round trip, because enthalpy is a state function.

Hess's law

Hess's law of constant heat summation

The total enthalpy change of a chemical reaction is the same whether the reaction takes place in one step or in several steps, provided the initial and final states are the same. \Delta H is independent of the path.

Hess's law is not a new law: it follows directly from the first law, because H is a state function and \Delta H depends only on the end points.

The three operations that solve every Hess problem:

  1. Add two equations and their \Delta H values add.
  2. Reverse an equation and the sign of \Delta H flips (Laplace's law).
  3. Multiply an equation by a number and \Delta H is multiplied by the same number.

Hess's law in three equations

Problem. Find \Delta H for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g), given (i) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), \Delta H = -393.5 kJ (ii) CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), \Delta H = -283.0 kJ.

Solution. The target has CO on the right and only ½O₂ used, so take (i) minus (ii): (i) gives CO₂ on the right; (ii) reversed puts CO₂ on the left and CO on the right with \Delta H = +283.0 kJ. Adding:

C(s) + O₂(g) + CO₂(g) → CO₂(g) + CO(g) + ½O₂(g)

Cancel CO₂ and ½O₂ from both sides: C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g) \Delta H = -393.5 + 283.0 = \mathbf{-110.5} kJ mol⁻¹.

Hess's law from formation enthalpies

Problem. Find \Delta H^\circ for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), using \Delta H_f^\circ: CH₄ −74.8, CO₂ −393.5, H₂O(l) −285.8 kJ mol⁻¹.

Solution. \Delta H^\circ = [(-393.5) + 2(-285.8)] - [(-74.8) + 2(0)] = (-393.5 - 571.6) + 74.8 = -965.1 + 74.8 = \mathbf{-890.3} kJ mol⁻¹. The two zeros are the O₂, an element in its standard state.

Forgetting them, or forgetting the coefficient 2 on water, are the two classic errors.

Hess's law round a three-equation cycle

Problem. Find \Delta H_f^\circ of ethyne, 2C(s) + H₂(g) → C₂H₂(g), from (i) C₂H₂(g) + 5/2O₂(g) → 2CO₂(g) + H₂O(l), \Delta H = -1299.5 kJ (ii) C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), \Delta H = -393.5 kJ (iii) H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) → H₂O(l), \Delta H = -285.8 kJ.

Solution. The target has C₂H₂ on the right, so (i) must be reversed (\Delta H = +1299.5). It also needs 2C on the left, so (ii) is doubled (\Delta H = -787.0). Hydrogen appears once, so (iii) is used as it stands.

Adding the three adjusted equations:

2C(s) + 2O₂(g) + H₂(g) + ½O₂(g) + 2CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) → 2CO₂(g) + H₂O(l) + C₂H₂(g) + 5/2O₂(g)

Cancel 2CO₂, H₂O(l) and 5/2O₂ from both sides (2 + ½ = 5/2 on the left):

2C(s) + H₂(g) → C₂H₂(g)

\Delta H = (+1299.5) + (-787.0) + (-285.8) = \mathbf{+226.7} kJ mol⁻¹.

The positive sign is the point: ethyne is endothermic with respect to its elements, which is why it is unstable, burns with a very hot flame and can decompose explosively. A negative answer here would mean an arithmetic slip in the reversal.

Hess problems in an MCQ

Do not balance anything you are not asked to balance. Look at where the target substance appears, decide "same side or opposite side", and add or subtract.

If the target has a coefficient of 2, double the whole equation and its \Delta H. Then check the sign with common sense: forming CO from elements must release heat, so the answer is negative.

11.3 Spontaneity, entropy and the second law; Gibbs free energy and its relation to the equilibrium constant

Spontaneity

A spontaneous process is one that has a natural tendency to occur once started, without outside help: a ball rolling downhill, iron rusting, gas expanding into a vacuum, ice melting above 0 °C.

Spontaneous does not mean fast — the conversion of diamond to graphite is spontaneous and takes longer than the age of the Earth.

Two driving forces decide spontaneity: the tendency to reach lower energy (exothermic, \Delta H < 0) and the tendency to reach greater disorder (entropy increase, \Delta S > 0). Neither alone is sufficient.

Entropy and the second law

Entropy

Entropy S is a measure of the disorder or randomness of a system — the number of ways its energy and particles can be arranged. Its unit is J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. For a reversible change at constant temperature, \Delta S = q_{\text{rev}}/T.

Change \Delta S Reason
Solid → liquid → gas positive particles become freer
Gas produced in a reaction positive moles of gas increase
Gas consumed negative moles of gas decrease
Mixing two gases positive more arrangements
Cooling a substance negative less thermal disorder

The third law fixes the zero: the entropy of a perfectly ordered crystal at 0 K is zero. That is why absolute entropies can be tabulated, while only changes in U and H can be measured.

The second law of thermodynamics

For any spontaneous change, the total entropy of the universe increases:

\Delta S_{\text{universe}} = \Delta S_{\text{system}} + \Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} > 0

For a reversible change it is zero; a negative total is impossible.

The entropy of the system alone may fall — freezing water is spontaneous below 0 °C even though \Delta S_{\text{system}} < 0 — because the heat released raises the entropy of the surroundings by more:

\Delta S_{\text{surroundings}} = -\frac{\Delta H}{T}

So a reaction is spontaneous when \Delta S_{\text{system}} - \Delta H/T > 0, which multiplied by -T gives the Gibbs criterion below.

Gibbs free energy

Gibbs free energy

G = H - TS. At constant temperature and pressure the change is

\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S

A process is spontaneous when \Delta G < 0, at equilibrium when \Delta G = 0, and non-spontaneous when \Delta G > 0.

\Delta G combines the two driving forces into one number: \Delta H is the heat term and -T\Delta S the disorder term, weighted by the temperature.

\Delta H \Delta S \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S Spontaneous? Example
− + always negative at all temperatures combustion of a fuel
− − negative at low T, positive at high T at low T freezing of water below 0 °C
+ + positive at low T, negative at high T at high T melting of ice; CaCO₃ decomposition
+ − always positive never 3O₂ → 2O₃ under ordinary conditions

The switch-over temperature, where \Delta G = 0, is

T = \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta S}

ΔG < 0 means spontaneous, not fast

A negative \Delta G says the reaction can go, not that it will go quickly.

Diamond → graphite has \Delta G < 0 and does not happen measurably; the conversion of sugar to CO₂ and water has \Delta G < 0 and needs a flame or an enzyme. Kinetics (Unit 9) decides the speed, thermodynamics the direction.

An option that equates "spontaneous" with "fast" or with "exothermic" is the commonest wrong key in this chapter.

Finding the temperature at which a reaction turns

Problem. For a reaction \Delta H = +50 kJ mol⁻¹ and \Delta S = +100 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. At what temperature does it become spontaneous?

Solution. Spontaneous needs \Delta G < 0, so T\Delta S > \Delta H: T > \frac{50\,000}{100} = \mathbf{500} K (227 °C). Above 500 K the disorder term outweighs the heat term. Below it, the reaction is non-spontaneous.

Free energy and the equilibrium constant

At equilibrium \Delta G = 0 and the reaction quotient equals K. Combining this with \Delta G = \Delta G^\circ + RT\ln Q gives the bridge between thermodynamics and equilibrium:

\Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K = -2.303RT\log K

\Delta G^\circ K Meaning
negative K > 1 products favoured at equilibrium
zero K = 1 reactants and products comparable
positive K < 1 reactants favoured at equilibrium

Note that K depends only on temperature, so \Delta G^\circ must be quoted at a stated temperature. A catalyst changes neither.

Equilibrium constant from ΔG°

Problem. A reaction has \Delta G^\circ = -20 kJ mol⁻¹ at 298 K. Find K (R = 8.314 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹).

Solution. \ln K = -\frac{\Delta G^\circ}{RT} = \frac{20\,000}{(8.314)(298)} = 8.07. K = e^{8.07} \approx \mathbf{3.2 \times 10^3}.

A large K, as expected from a strongly negative \Delta G^\circ: every 5.7 kJ mol⁻¹ of \Delta G^\circ changes K by a factor of ten at room temperature.

ΔG at a temperature other than 298 K

Problem. For N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g), \Delta H^\circ = -92.4 kJ mol⁻¹ and \Delta S^\circ = -198 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Find \Delta G^\circ at 298 K and at 700 K.

Solution. At 298 K: \Delta G^\circ = -92.4 - (298)(-0.198) = -92.4 + 59.0 = \mathbf{-33.4} kJ mol⁻¹ (spontaneous).

At 700 K: \Delta G^\circ = -92.4 - (700)(-0.198) = -92.4 + 138.6 = \mathbf{+46.2} kJ mol⁻¹ (non-spontaneous at standard pressure).

This is exactly why the Haber process is run at about 700 K only with a pressure of 200 atm: the high pressure makes Q small, so the actual \Delta G stays negative even though \Delta G^\circ has changed sign.

Temperature helps the rate and hurts the yield; pressure rescues the yield.

Chapter summary

  • A system is open, closed or isolated; only an isolated system has \Delta U = 0 always. U, H, S and G are state functions; q and w are path functions whose sum alone is fixed.
  • Extensive properties scale with amount (mass, U, H, S, G); intensive ones do not (T, P, density, molar enthalpy).
  • First law (IUPAC): \Delta U = q + w, with q positive into the system and w = -P\Delta V positive when work is done on it. An expanding gas has negative work.
  • H = U + PV; \Delta H = q_p at constant pressure and \Delta U = q_v at constant volume; \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_g RT.
  • \Delta H_f^\circ is zero only for an element in its standard state; \Delta H^\circ_{\text{rxn}} is products minus reactants.
  • Combustion is always exothermic; neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is −57.1 kJ mol⁻¹; fusion and vaporisation are always endothermic, and \Delta H_{\text{sub}} = \Delta H_{\text{fus}} + \Delta H_{\text{vap}}.
  • Laplace's law: reversing a reaction reverses the sign of \Delta H. Hess's law: \Delta H is path-independent, so equations can be added, reversed and multiplied.
  • Second law: \Delta S_{\text{universe}} > 0 for a spontaneous change; \Delta S_{\text{surr}} = -\Delta H/T, so an exothermic reaction can be spontaneous even when its own entropy falls.
  • \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S: negative spontaneous, zero equilibrium, positive non-spontaneous; T = \Delta H/\Delta S is the switch-over temperature; spontaneous never means fast.
  • \Delta G^\circ = -RT\ln K: a negative \Delta G^\circ gives K > 1; K depends only on temperature.

Model answer D1: first law, enthalpy and Hess's law (10 marks)

Introduction. A system is the part of the universe under study. It may be open, closed or isolated. A state function (U, H, S, G, P, V, T) depends only on the state, while heat q and work w are path functions.

First law. Energy can be neither created nor destroyed: \Delta U = q + w (IUPAC sign convention: q and w are positive when added to the system). For expansion against an external pressure, w = -P\Delta V.

Enthalpy. H = U + PV, so \Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V and for gases \Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_gRT. At constant pressure \Delta H = q_p and at constant volume \Delta U = q_v. A reaction is exothermic if \Delta H < 0 and endothermic if \Delta H > 0.

Types of enthalpy: formation (\Delta_fH^{\circ}, zero for elements in the standard state), combustion, neutralisation (-57.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} for a strong acid and strong base), atomisation, bond dissociation, lattice enthalpy and solution.

Hess's law. The total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same whether it takes place in one step or in several steps, because H is a state function.

Two uses: \Delta_rH^{\circ} = \sum\Delta_fH^{\circ}(\text{products}) - \sum\Delta_fH^{\circ}(\text{reactants}) and \Delta_rH = \sum(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum(\text{bonds formed}).

The Born-Haber cycle applies Hess's law to find lattice enthalpy.

Heat capacity relation Formula
Heat change q = mc\Delta T
Gases C_p - C_v = R
Kirchhoff \Delta H_2 - \Delta H_1 = \Delta C_p(T_2 - T_1)

Numerical. For CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O(l), with \Delta_fH^{\circ} of -74.8, -393.5 and -285.8\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} for CH₄, CO₂ and H₂O: \Delta_rH^{\circ} = [-393.5 + 2(-285.8)] - [-74.8] = -890.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}.

Burning 16\ \text{g} of methane releases 890\ \text{kJ}. Also, \Delta U = \Delta H - \Delta n_gRT, with \Delta n_g = 1 - 3 = -2 here, which gives \Delta U = -890.3 + 2(8.314)(298)/1000 = -885.3\ \text{kJ}.

Conclusion. Hess's law lets us find the enthalpy of any reaction from tabulated formation enthalpies, because enthalpy is a state function.

Model answer D2: entropy, Gibbs energy and spontaneity (10 marks)

Introduction. Many spontaneous processes are exothermic, but some endothermic processes are spontaneous too (melting of ice above 0^{\circ}\text{C}, dissolving of NH₄NO₃). The additional factor is the disorder, measured by entropy.

Entropy S. A measure of the randomness of a system, \Delta S = \dfrac{q_{rev}}{T} (J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). It increases for solid → liquid → gas and when moles of gas increase.

Second law: in a spontaneous process, the entropy of the universe increases: \Delta S_{total} = \Delta S_{sys} + \Delta S_{surr} > 0. Third law: the entropy of a perfect crystal at 0\ \text{K} is zero.

Gibbs free energy. G = H - TS, and at constant T and P:

\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S

\Delta H \Delta S \Delta G Spontaneity
negative positive always negative spontaneous at all temperatures
positive negative always positive non-spontaneous at all temperatures
negative negative negative at low T spontaneous at low temperature
positive positive negative at high T spontaneous at high temperature

At equilibrium \Delta G = 0, so T = \Delta H/\Delta S. Also \Delta G^{\circ} = -RT\ln K, so a large K means a negative \Delta G^{\circ}. The maximum non-expansion work obtainable from a process is -\Delta G.

Other points. (1) For a phase change at its transition temperature, \Delta S = \Delta H/T (for example \Delta S_{fus} of ice = 6010/273 = 22\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}). (2) Entropy of the surroundings is -\Delta H/T.

(3) The Gibbs energy of formation of an element is zero.

Numerical. For CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), \Delta H^{\circ} = +178\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1} and \Delta S^{\circ} = +160.5\ \text{J K}^{-1}\text{mol}^{-1}. At 298\ \text{K}, \Delta G = 178 - 298\times0.1605 = +130\ \text{kJ}, non-spontaneous.

The reaction becomes spontaneous above T = \dfrac{178\,000}{160.5} = 1109\ \text{K} (about 836^{\circ}\text{C}), which is why limestone is heated in a kiln.

Conclusion. \Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S combines the energy and disorder factors and shows how temperature can switch a reaction from non-spontaneous to spontaneous.
